name: Miri
confidence_why: Needham 1886 and Doley 2023 put main stress on the penultimate syllable of Sa:yang Mising (the first syllable of the usual two-syllable word), but Taid 1987, Pegu 2010 and Pagag 2017 put it on the second syllable, Pagag for the same Sa:yang dialect, so comparable modern first-hand descriptions disagree on where the main stress falls.

new_statements.translation: In the Pagro dialect the primary stress generally falls on the initial syllable of the word. As a result of primary stress on the initial syllable, gemination of the syllable coda is observed. (p. 100) | In two-syllable words the primary stress generally falls on the first syllable of the word. ... [quoting Padun:] In words with more than two syllables the stress falls on the penultimate syllable. (Padun 75) (p. 227) | In the Sa:yang dialect the primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the word, and in the Pagro dialect on the initial syllable of the word. Because stress falls on the initial syllable in Pagro, the following consonant is geminated. (p. 315) | Mising is not a tone language. (p. 106)

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record (penultimate stress = penultimate) rests on Needham 1886, which describes Shaiyang (= Sa:yang) Miri. Doley's Sa:yang chapter and her ch. V comparison give exactly penultimate stress for Sa:yang (agrees, same dialect), and add that the other main dialect, Pagro (with Dolu, Oyan), has fixed initial stress with post-tonic gemination and medial-vowel deletion — a dialect difference that the catalog does not record; for disyllables the two placements coincide, so the difference shows only in words of three or more syllables (e.g. vocative ni:'nia Sa:yang vs 'na:na Pagro). Also confirms no lexical tone.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Dialect-split. Sa:yang (= the catalog's Shaiyang variety): primary stress on the penultimate syllable — first syllable in disyllables ('a:mi 'person', 'ɨki 'dog', 'ɨmɨ 'fire', 'ɨkum 'house'), penult in longer words (Padun 75), shown by suffixed vocatives ni:ni+a > ni:'nia, ka:kɨ+a > ka:'kɨa. Pagro (and Dolu, Oyan): primary stress on the initial syllable regardless of length, with gemination of the following consonant (sitɨ > 'sittɨ 'elephant', tabɨ > 'tabbɨ 'snake') and deletion of the medial vowel in suffixed forms (na:ni+a > 'na:na). Stress is a weak, non-lexical feature; meaning is changed by sentence stress and intonation, not by word stress. Mising has no lexical tone (Grierson's tone claim rejected, p. 106).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed for words. Sentence stress: one primary stress per phrase in long sentences (p. 101, citing Goswami 2: 123); emphatic sentence stress can move to any word and shifts meaning (pp. 101, 228).
new_statements.exceptions: Pagro: loanwords also take initial stress (misa > 'mitsɨ, sãsa > 'otsɨ, p. 101). Sa:yang: suffixed/vocative words stress the middle (penultimate) syllable where Pagro/Dolu stress the initial one (pp. 227-228); Sa:yang shows none of the Pagro post-stress gemination (no sittɨ, dɨnnɨ, gunnɨ; p. 228, p. 315).
new_statements.identity_note: Doley 2023 describes two Mising dialects, Pagro (Majuli, Lakhimpur, Jorhat, Dhemaji, Sivasagar, Golaghat, Biswanath districts of Assam and Namsai, Arunachal) and Sa:yang, and mentions Dolu and Oyan as patterning with Pagro. The catalog's source (Needham 1886) is Shaiyang Miri = Doley's Sa:yang. Her stress findings are dialect-specific: Sa:yang penultimate, Pagro initial.

readall_conflicts: Within Doley 2023 there is no internal contradiction but a dialect split: Sa:yang = penultimate primary stress (p. 315; disyllables initial, longer words penult per Padun 75, p. 227), Pagro/Dolu/Oyan = initial primary stress with gemination of the following consonant (pp. 100, 315). The catalog's penultimate rule comes from Needham 1886 on Shaiyang (= Sa:yang) Miri, so the catalog and Doley agree on that variety; Doley's Pagro initial-stress statement differs from the catalog rule only for words of three or more syllables. Context from files a previous pass left held by the project in the same check folder (not in my works list): Taid 1987 (sec. 8) says word stress is weak and 'realized consistently in the second syllable'; Pegu 2010 (pegu2010/, sec. 2.1.2.4) says the second syllable of a disyllabic foot is stressed unless a heavy (long-vowel) syllable attracts it; Pagag 2017 (pagag2017/, sec. 3.5) says disyllabic morphemes are stressed on the second syllable — these second-syllable claims for disyllables contradict both Doley's initial-stress disyllables and Needham/the catalog's penult for disyllables. On tone, Doley (p. 106), Taid 1987 and Pegu 2010 say Mising is not tonal, whereas Prasad 1991 (sec. 1.5, p. 34) posits three distinctive tones.

audit.recode_to: From 'fixed penult, right edge, weight-blind, recomputed under suffixation' to 'weak stress on the second syllable (left-edge iamb), not shifting under suffixation (Taid 1987: ap'pi:, ap'pi:-ko, ap'pi:-ko-laŋ), with long vowels attracting stress ('i.sor vs ta.'ke:, Pegu 2010)'; keep Needham 1886 as a dated dialect-specific (Sa:yang) minority report in caution/contra, and drop what counts as heavy 'not-applicable'/weight-blind. If the schema cannot express weight-sensitive to-length + peninitial, at minimum flag kind as contested and add Taid 1987 / Pegu 2010 to 'contra'.

sources.citation: Taid, Tabu. 1987. A short note on Mising phonology. Linguistics of the Tibeto-Burman Area 10(1): 130-137.
sources.quote: "Word-stress is rather weak in Mising. The stress is realized consistently in the second syllable. Examples are: /a"ppi:/ /a"ppi:ko/ /a"ppi:kolang/ /a"ppi:komi' lo:min/. ... Mising is not a tone language." (stress stays on the 2nd syllable as suffixes are added: ap-PI:-ko-lang, not penult)
sources.note: Native-speaker phonology note; p.137 states weak stress fixed on the 2nd syllable and shows it NOT shifting under suffixation (a"ppi:, a"ppi:ko, a"ppi:kolang) - directly contradicts the Needham-based penult/right-edge coding.
